en: The Proof of God.
Accompanied by the commentary named *Siddhāñjana*.
(Sūtra: In this regard, the entire universe proceeds under the control of a certain One.
Thus, in order to establish this, we shall first set forth the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa). // 1 //

Regarding this, the Mīmāṃsakas say: "This person endowed with the power to perceive all objects does not deserve to be accepted, because he falls outside the scope of any possible means of valid cognition that could establish him, and because there are clear and manifold subverting arguments against him.
For instance, would his proof be perception or something else?"
Is perception (*pratyakṣa*) also worldly (*laukika*) or technical (*yaugika*)? (Commentary:
Having meditated upon the feet of Śrīpati and bowed to the pair of lotus-feet of my teacher, I compose this elegant exposition of the *Īśvarasiddhi* for the sake of easy understanding. (1)

May the Lord, established by the conclusion of the three Vedas and constantly contemplated with sound reasoning by those who investigate logic, become manifest through the practice of meditative devotion and extend to me pure wisdom. (2)
Then indeed, the venerable supreme teacher, the illustrious Bhagavad-Yāmunamuni, having performed reflection upon the self in the *Ātmasiddhi*,

and now performing reflection upon the Supreme Self in the *Īśvarasiddhi*, begins by undertaking the establishment of the means of valid cognition that prove the existence of God, stating "In that regard... (*tatra*).

The meaning of the verse is as follows: in order to establish— through valid means of knowledge— that the entire universe, consisting of both sentient and insentient entities, exists and functions entirely dependent upon the will of the one Lord of All (the *sarveśvara*)— that is, it proceeds by His will characterized as *saṅkalpa*, remaining established in its own unmixed forms and natures, and proceeding in its respective activities according to their proper order— we shall first describe the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).

In this context, because of the use of the pronoun *tatra* (there) which refers back to something previously mentioned, one may infer that there was some portion of a work on the proof of God (*īśvarasiddhi*) preceding this,
which has long since been lost. First of all,
what is established here is not the worldly [reality].
Therefore, there is no proof for that [existence], because all objects and the cognition thereof and so forth are not established.

For one who intends to convey [the existence of] a being endowed with the power to perceive all objects, every single object—whether separated by space, time, or nature, or obscured by a barrier—must be brought within the range of that perception and its power. However, since ordinary perception functions only upon a limited number of objects currently capable of sensory contact, such infinite majesty cannot even be a subject of possibility; how then can we consider it a means of proof in this context?

"'This is not [the case]': the meaning is that a specific conscious entity designated by the term 'Īśvara'—endowed with the power to directly perceive all objects and to produce all effects—is not fit to be accepted, due to the absence of proof and the force of refutation.
Regarding the phrase 'having passed beyond':"
*Atipatitā* means that from which all possibility of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for any practitioner has departed; such is the ground, which is the object.
*Tattvāt* means "because it is an object characterized by the departure of all possibility of the means of valid cognition for any practitioner.
Here, the reading is likely either *'atipatitasakalasādhakapramāṇasaṃbhāvanābhūmitvatvāt'* or *'atipatitasakalasādhakapramāṇasaṃbhāvanābhūmitvatvāt'*.
Regarding the word "sphuṭe":
it means that [the proof] is such because its various refutations (bādhaka) are "sphuṭa"—that is, well-known (prasiddha).
Having thus introduced both the absence of proof and the presence of refutation regarding the Lord (īśvara), he begins first to establish the absence of proof with the words "tathā hi" and so forth.
"Other" refers to inference and so forth.
He establishes that worldly perception—arising from the contact of the sense organs with their objects—is not a proof for the existence of God by means of the phrase "being established.
This qualifying attribute contains a logical reason (hetugarbha).
The meaning is: because the objects of worldly perception are limited and fixed;
"here" refers to the subject of God.
The means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) is that which accomplishes; that is to say, it is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). By that—namely, by worldly direct perception (*laukika-pratyakṣa*).
"Because of non-establishment"—that is, because of non-manifestation.

The meaning is this: for visual perception (*cākṣuṣa-pratyakṣa*), the objects are only color (*rūpa*), things possessing color (*rūpin*), and number (*saṅkhyā*) and so forth which are inherent in the same object as color;
they are not taste (*rasa*) and so forth. Thus, there is limitation (*parimitatā*).

Only form that is manifested and not overwhelmed, and which has magnitude as its single locus, is to be apprehended—not that which resides in atoms and the like; thus, there too, the rule is established.
This should be understood to apply to gustatory perception and the others as well.
And since such sensory perception does not illuminate all objects and so forth, it cannot constitute a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding God.
For that [perceiver] is intended to be distinguished by the capacity to effect the perception of all objects;
yet, without the perception of the object, its apprehension, and its power, the apprehension of that [perceiver] is not possible,
because [the perceiver] includes even those things unfit for all objects, and because power is beyond the reach of the senses.
Since cognition is not graspable by the external senses, and since external objects are not grasped by the mind alone, there is no apprehension of any object whatsoever by any sense organ.
And without the apprehension of those [objects], there can be no apprehension of the qualified Lord (viśiṣṭeśvara),
according to the logical principle that "that which has a qualifier [the viśeṣaṇa] cannot be apprehended if the qualifier itself is not apprehended."
Therefore, sensory perception, which is worldly in nature, cannot be a means of valid cognition regarding God. // 2 //
Nor is the perception of a yogin a proof for this [self], because—being perceptual, it too has only the presently existing as its object;
it does not have the past and so forth as its object, just like a mental intuition (pratibhā) and the like. (3)
Now, is that cognition of the yogin sensory or non-sensory?
Even if it is sensory, does it arise from the external sense organs or from the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)?
It is well known in the world that the external sense organs generate cognitions regarding their respective objects only when assisted by contact with those very objects.
Therefore, there is no consequence of perceiving all objects— such as those that are unarisen, past, or obstructed— by means of the sense of taste and so forth;
nor is contact possible with non-existent things like the unarisen and so on, because contact depends upon two substrata and is impossible when such substrata are absent.
Therefore, the contact with the object is required.
In the absence of auxiliary causes, how could the sense organs be capable of directly perceiving objects that are past and so forth?
And it is the case that whatever has a certain auxiliary cause for the production of a certain effect, [that cause is necessary for that effect].
In the absence of those [auxiliaries], that [cause] does not produce its effect;

for example, a seed which produces the effect of a sprout when assisted by earth and water does not produce a sprout in the absence of earth and so forth. Since the external sense-faculties produce cognition only when assisted by contact with an object, they too do not produce cognition regarding an object that is past or future. Therefore, the perception produced by them does not transgress the aforementioned restriction regarding its object.
Nor is the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) possible [as the instrument], because [the self] possesses independence with respect to pleasure and so forth, which are exclusively internal objects;
for if one were to admit that the mind has unrestrained instrumental power over external objects, then the eyes and other [senses] would be rendered useless.
And for this reason, no one would be blind or deaf.

Regarding this, there is the following argument: the mind, when it is a point of dispute, does not function toward the domain of external perception independently of the external sense organs, because its operation therein is dependent upon them.

Whatever functions in dependence upon a certain condition does not function there independently of it, just as the eye, whose functioning depends upon light, does not function in its own domain when there is blinding darkness. Nor is it possible that the sense organs— which have attained excellence through the power of perfected medicines, mantras, and meditative absorption (*samādhi*)— should ever abandon the restriction regarding objects established by that meditative absorption.
Because the sole fruit of those [means] is the manifestation of an innate capacity,
and because that capacity is restricted [to specific objects],
the ear— even when refined by a hundred well-administered medicines— is certainly not capable of perceiving the distinction between color and taste.

And there is this [inference]: "The excellence of proficiency in the external and internal instruments under discussion in the debate does not transcend its limits, because it is an excellence of sensory perception, like the excellence of that [perception] currently being observed"; thus, sensory cognition does not have the past and so forth as its object.

However, for that which arises from the ultimate limit of the intensification of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), even though it possesses a clear appearance, since it determines its object as either more or less than what was the domain of the prior experience, it revolves within the whirlpools of either memory or delusion; how, then, could it attain the shore of validity? And how much less could it be established as perception (*pratyakṣa*)?

Or, if [the Lord] were indeed possessed of perception, how could there be a transgression of the restriction regarding the objects known by it? Or, if he were to transgress it, how could he possess the status of perception? Thus, perception is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) with respect to the Lord, who possesses the sovereignty of universal experience.
(This concludes the refutation of perception as a means of knowledge regarding the Lord.)
Nor is it another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*).
Is it inference (*anumāna*) or scripture (*āgama*)?
If it is inference, is it "inference from the particular" (*viśeṣatodṛṣṭa*) or "inference from the general" (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*)?

In that regard, since the Blessed One is so far removed from the path of all [empirical] means of knowledge, this inference is not capable of arising; for it arises dependent upon the ascertainment of an invariable concomitance preceded by the direct perception of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) [of the probans].
Indeed, those who have never perceived fire before are unable to connect smoke with it as being invariably concomitant.
Furthermore, no logical mark (*liṅga*), even one based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*), is found that is capable of directly perceiving the manifestation of all objects.
(Thus is the introduction to the impossibility of inference being a means of valid cognition regarding God.
He himself explains the meaning of the verse beginning with "vyavasthite" by saying "sarvārtha":
"avagamayatā" means "grasping."
The reading "avagamayanta" found in earlier printed editions is incorrect.
"Spatial remoteness" (deśaviprakarṣa) means being situated in a distant place;
"temporal remoteness" (kālaviprakarṣa) refers to being past or future.
Remoteness by nature consists in unfitness, which takes the form of being beyond the senses.
It is observed that even for things that are otherwise fit, there is non-perception by the eyes and other senses when they are obstructed by walls and the like.
The point is that such objects are included among all possible objects.
The particle *eva* has the sense of "also.
"To be made objects" (*gocarayitavyāni*) means "to be made into spheres of perception" (*viṣayīkaraṇīyāni*).
This is a grammatical indication using a neuter singular remainder (*klībaikaśeṣa*), according to the rule "the neuter remains when combined with non-neuters."
Regarding the phrase "na ce" (and not):
by the term "existing," there is the exclusion of that which is remote in time;
by the term "capable of sensory contact," there is the exclusion of that which is obstructed and that which is remote in space.
By the word "katipaya" (some), that which is beyond the senses is indicated.
"Having a function restricted to some objects" means possessing an operation conducive to grasping only those specific categories of things mentioned above.
"Unbounded greatness" refers to excellence that is not co-located with any degree of deficiency.
And that [nature] consists in the fact that knowledge has all objects as its domain. "That" refers to worldly perception;
"here" refers to God, who is distinguished by such qualities as omniscience.
The proof is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
The rest is clear.
He establishes that even the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of a yogin does not prove the existence of God with the words "because it is direct perception."

Since grasping a present object is pervaded by being perception (*pratyakṣa*), if the cognition of a yogin were also perception, it would have to grasp only the present; thus, it would not possess the capacity to grasp all objects.
Alternatively, if its objects were the past and so forth, it would not be perception.

However, the meaning is that God, like knowledge consisting of intuition (*pratibhā*) and so forth, is merely a specific form of presented cognition (*upanītabhāna*) that is susceptible to doubt and other defects; therefore, He is not capable of attaining the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). //3//
Indeed, the world under dispute is dependent on a single conscious being, because it is composed of non-conscious matter, like one's own healthy body. // 4 //
Likewise, let the skill in directly realizing the manifestation of all objects be inferred from the Creator of the world, precisely because the world is an effect. (5)

For every effect— such as a pot, a water-jar, a palace, and so forth— is understood to be fashioned by a conscious agent who perceives the material cause, the instruments, the recipient, and the purpose;
and since the subject of dispute, such as the earth, mountains, and great oceans, is also an effect, it too is determined to have a conscious intelligent cause of that same nature.

Nor should it be said that its being an effect is unestablished, for that is established by reasons such as the arrangement of parts (*avayava-sanniveśa*). Here, everything from the ultimate composite wholes (*antyāvayavin*) down to the dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) is understood to be produced by specific conjunctions of various parts that decrease in size; thus, in the end, the material cause (*upādāna*) is of four kinds.
The atoms are the material cause of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*).

Their initial motion has as its non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) the conjunction of those respective individual souls (*kṣetrajña*) with their own specific unseen merit or demerit (*adṛṣṭa*). Furthermore, the instruments are the unseen forces (*adṛṣṭa*) characterized as merit and demerit residing in all individual souls.
The purpose, moreover, consists in the various modes of assistance to sentient beings, which take the form of diverse causal activities brought about by that [initial motion].
Those very field-knower (*kṣetrajña*) beings who enjoy those [fruits] are the recipients (*sampradāna*).

Furthermore, these [beings] are not capable of perceiving even their own inherent merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*); therefore, there must exist one who transcends them—an Ishvara who is skilled in the creation of the entire universe, whose unsurpassed innate sovereignty over the cognition of all objects is established as a *siddhānta* by the nature of the case (*adhikaraṇasiddhānta*), and whose power is beyond measure.

"Why is the preeminent Person (*puruṣadhaureya*) not inferred from a mark characterized by general observation? (This is the demonstration of the validity of inference based on general observation regarding God.
The Mīmāṃsakas mock this, saying: "This is merely the flash of a fickle argument constructed by one's own mind, belonging to someone who does not understand the actual workings of inference."
For instance— what is intended by this "dependence on a single conscious being" regarding the body, the world, and so forth?
If it means "subordination to that [being]," then he elaborates upon the very meaning of the verse with the words beginning with "tat" (that).

The compound beginning with "samadhigate" is a *bahuvrīhi*. It refers to the eyes and other sense organs by which the auxiliary cause consisting of the contact with their respective appropriate objects has been attained.
The meaning is that it is well known in the world that [the senses] produce perceptual cognitions of their own respective objects.
Regarding the word "therefore" (*ata*):
because the auxiliary nature (*sahakāritva*) of the contact with the object is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
The meaning is "therefore.
Regarding the phrase "by means of the tongue and so forth," the reading might alternatively be "by means of the eyes and so forth."
Regarding "ajātātivṛttau" (in the case of the unborn and the past): this refers to the future and the past.
He establishes that the absence of contact (*sannikarṣābhāva*) is the cause for the senses not apprehending the past and the future with the words "na ca" ("and not").
As for the reading "rajatādibhiḥ" (by means of silver, etc.), it is not well-construed.
Because that proximity, characterized by conjunction, has two substrata— that is, it inheres in both—
there would be an absence of the substratum [of cognition] if either one of the two substrata were missing.
"Because that is impossible"—that is, because contact cannot arise.
"Therefore" means "because [the sense organ] acts as a cooperative cause.
He establishes the impossibility of the sense organ apprehending the past and so forth by stating "cooperative cause."

The meaning is that "due to the absence of the cause, there is the absence of the effect. He elaborates on this point by setting it forth in the form of a formal syllogism (prayoga) with the words "And if... and so forth; the phrase beginning with "That which... is the statement of the example (udāharaṇa).

The term *yatsahakārī* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has such-and-such a cooperative cause. The sense is: "distinguished by such-and-such a cooperative cause. This should be understood in the same way for what follows as well.
"Jananam" means "the producer.
"Upon the contact with the object," and so forth, is the application (*upanaya*).
"Those too," and so forth, is the conclusion (*nigamana*).

The thesis and the reason— "the sense faculties do not apprehend [objects] that are past and so forth, because they are not in contact with them"— should be understood accordingly. Thus, it has been stated that if the perception of a yogin were produced by external sense faculties, it would not have all things as its object.
Consequently, it follows that its status as a means of proof (*sādhana*) regarding God is untenable.

Now, even if it were produced by the mind alone, he states "nor internal" (*nāpyāntare*) to show that it lacks the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) precisely because it does not grasp all objects.
"Internal object" (*āntaragocara*) [refers to this].
This is a *karmadhāraya* compound.
The meaning is that [the mind] produces perception only with respect to non-external objects such as pleasure and the like, by not being made to operate through the external sense organs.
He states the fault in the mind directly grasping external objects with the words "niraṅkuśe" (unrestrained).
In this context, "unrestrainedness" (niraṅkuśatva) means independence from the external sense-faculties.

Having thus established the reason (*hetu*) with respect to the mind, he establishes the probandum (*sādhya*) by way of a formal argument (*prayoga*), [concluding] with the word "it occurs" (*bhavati*).
The word "formal argument" (*prayoga*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
It does not proceed, nor does it possess an activity conducive to apprehension,

because its operation is dependent [on something else]— that is, because it possesses the functional activity of apprehension by means of the cooperation of the external sense-faculties with respect to external objects.
"Dependent" (*tantra*) means that which is the instigator (*prayojaka*).
Or it is that which has a cooperative cause; that whose activity is dependent on such [a cause] is "that which has an activity dependent on that" (tattantravṛtti).
The etymology is as follows: "tattva" is that which has the nature (bhāva) of "tat" (that); therefore, it is so called. An example is the phrase "yadi atra" (if here).

The meaning is as follows: if, in a given effect, something possesses an operation whose production depends upon the presence of a particular auxiliary cause, then in the absence of that [auxiliary], it does not possess the capacity to produce that effect; for example, the eye, which requires light as an auxiliary, does not produce the visual perception of its object—such as a jar—in the absence of light.
[The opponent] raises an objection with the words "na ca" (and not).
Even the capacity established from birth is not mentioned separately here because it is the fruit of past austerity (*tapas*).

The extraordinary sharpness of the sense organs (*indriya*)—which is achieved through perfected medicines and the like—is characterized by the power to perceive subtle, remote, and other such objects. "Having attained a restriction regarding their objects" means having attained the natural (*autsargika*) restriction consisting in the grasping of only those objects that are present, suitable, and proximate.

They abandon—meaning they relinquish—and avoid it. Regarding the phrase "inborn" (*sāṃsiddhika*): the very nature of perfected elixirs and the like is to expand the innate capacity of the instruments of action, whose functioning was previously contracted due to being bound by karma.
The meaning is that [the sense organs] do not possess the capacity to produce a new [transcendental] power (*apūrva-śakti*).
Now, let it be so; even then, what does this have to do with the fact that all objects are not apprehended by the yogic eye and other such faculties?
Regarding this, he says: "And because of capacity.
For the inherent capacity of the eye is only for the apprehension of color-form and the like;
it does not mean that its capacity for the apprehension of taste and so forth is possible even through yoga or other means. This is the meaning.
And thus, although the yogic eye may indeed perceive even the most subtle form of fire due to its extreme acuity,
the point is that it does not thereby become a perceiver of the past or of taste and so forth.
He states the reasoning for this with the words "it happens."

"Without transgressing the boundary" means not overstepping its own limits. And the limit [of the eye] is its function as the grasper of form alone among the four [objects], such as visible form and so forth. The same should be understood for the tongue and the other [senses] as well.
Regarding the phrase "as it is seen":
for even non-yogis, a gradation in the perception of form and so forth is observed due to the intensity or dullness of their visual light.

The intention is that, in the same way, although the intensity of the yogi’s visual light would have a range greater than that [of ordinary vision], it is established as being strictly within its own limits and not transcending them.

Having thus established that yogic cognition cannot grasp all objects if it were sensory, [the author] now establishes its true nature even if it were non-sensory, and for that very reason, the impossibility of it being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding God, with the words "bhāvanā" and so forth.
It is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning: "that whose birth arises from the culmination of cultivation (*bhāvanā*)."
In "possessing a clear manifestation"— that is, in possessing a clear illumination— there is the characterization of being an object of worldly experience.
From "the domain of prior experience"— that is, from the object of a previous experience—
it "determines," meaning it illuminates.
The meaning is this: if the object is not greater than what was previously experienced, it is a memory;
however, if the object is greater, it is an error, like the perception of a woman as being present before one who is imagining a beloved woman when she is actually non-existent.
This is the collective intention: through the repeated practice of recollecting what has been experienced, an accumulation of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) is achieved.

When that culminating practice of recollection occurs, the memory that arises possesses a manifestation of its object so clear that it is as if it were direct perception; thus, if it is precisely this memory—having a form identical to direct perception—that is intended to be the "direct perception of the yogi" (*yogipratyakṣa*), [then there is no fault].
In that case, because it has as its object only an object previously experienced, it does not have the Lord as its object;
for the Lord, who is capable of grasping all objects and so forth, was never previously experienced due to the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) [to perceive Him].
Furthermore, if it were a memory, it could not possibly possess validity, whether defined as being an experience of an object as it truly is, or defined as making known an object not already known.
For this very reason, it is all the more impossible for that [knowledge] to have the nature of perception, which is a specific type of valid cognition (*pramāṇaviśeṣa*);
thus [it says], "if it were perception."
The summary of the meaning of the verse is "or of perception" (*pratyakṣasya vā*).
"Being known" (*viditatva*) means being well-established (*prasiddhatva*).
"Not all" (*na viśve*).

With respect to the Lord—who is the direct perceiver of all, the creator of all, and the controller of all—sensory perception, whether belonging to people like us or to yogis, is not a means of valid cognition; that is to say, it does not produce valid knowledge. Now, one might object: even if [the internal organ] is independent regarding external objects only in its ordinary state, its activity toward external, supersensuous, and temporally remote objects is indeed possible when it is assisted by the preeminent unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) born of yoga. Therefore, the perception produced by the mind assisted by that preeminent *adṛṣṭa* would belong to yogis and could serve as a means of valid cognition regarding the Lord.

If it is argued that the established rule—that perception grasps only the present—is restricted solely to the domain of non-yogic perception, we reply as follows: even through the assistance of a preeminent and extraordinary unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), there may indeed be the apprehension of all objects according to valid means of knowledge;
however, there is no proof whatsoever for a single, omniscient Lord.
Therefore, the intention of the objector is that its establishment does not occur even through yogic perception (*yogaja-pratyakṣa*).

By this, the view that mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*) concerning the Supreme Self—produced precisely by meditation (*dhyāna*) upon the Supreme Self—is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding Him is also refuted;
for meditation upon the Supreme Self is indeed impossible without prior knowledge of Him.
And ultimately, it must be stated that this [knowledge] is produced solely by the scripture;
yet, for a scripture whose primary purpose is action, there is no intentionality (*tātparya*) regarding that [ontological reality].

Furthermore, in the view that the Veda is of human origin, the circularity (*anyonyasaṃśraya*) is quite evident: the authority of the scripture is established because it was spoken by God, and the existence of God is established because of what is stated in that [scripture].
And upon the establishment of that [the world], the existence of God is established;
however, it will be stated immediately hereafter that inference is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in this regard.
Thus, since there is an absolute absence of any valid cognition of God, the meditation and other practices based upon Him are likewise unestablished.
Thus it has been stated that neither kind of perception—whether worldly (laukika) or yogic (yaugika)—serves as a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) regarding God.
What, then, would depend upon Him? Is it His birth, or His subsistence, or His activity?
In the case of the first two [birth and subsistence], the illustrative example lacks the property to be proven (sādhyahīna).
Indeed, the body is not produced and maintained by the volition of a single conscious being.

For those who partake in the experience of pleasure and pain dependent upon a particular body, all of them— provided they possess the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) appropriate for that— become the cause of its production and maintenance, just like the possessor of that body.
Moreover, the stability of a whole body, characterized by its inherence in its own parts, does not depend on any external conscious agent apart from a specific interlocking of those parts.

However, as for that stability characterized by vital breath which does depend on such an agent, it is not possible in the case of the earth and other elements under discussion; thus, we do not observe even "stability" to be of a uniform nature that follows both the subject and the similar instances.

However, if [the world] were to function under the dependence of a single volition, there would be a deviation from the rule in the case of stones, trees, chariots, and so forth, which are moved by the forceful efforts of many powerful people.
Furthermore, since this probandum is already established by the mere fact of being "begun" (*ārabdhatva*), this mention of a specific material cause (*upādānaviśeṣa*) is redundant.
He clarifies the manner in which the specific form of the intended Lord is established by this inference with the word "all."
The material cause is the *upādāna*;
the instrumental cause is the *upakaraṇa*;
and the recipient is the *saṃpradāna*, which is the effect created for the purpose of experience.
He is the enjoyer. The purpose is the fruit to be accomplished by the object being produced.

The meaning is that a produced effect, such as a jar and so forth, is seen to be made by means of a conscious being who is the perceiver—the direct witness—of the material causes and other factors; that conscious being serves as the efficient cause (nimitta-hetu).
A *maṇika* is a large water-jar.
By this statement, it is established that the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*) is pervaded by the property of having an agent (*sakartṛkatva*).

Here, "agency" (*kartṛtva*) is intended to mean the possession of immediate (*aparokṣa*) knowledge, desire to act (*cikīrṣā*), and volitional effort (*kṛti*) directed toward the material cause (*upādāna*) and other factors.

In the definition of the *upanaya* (application), it is stated: "and [it must be] something not already established. The term "subject of dispute" (*vimatipada*) refers to that which has become the object of conflicting views regarding its having an author or lacking an author.
By this, it is indicated that the status of being a *pakṣa* (the subject of inference), characterized by having a probandum that is still doubtful, is established for the earth and so forth.
Anticipating the objection that the reason is unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddhi*), he refutes it with the words "And not" (*na ca*).
The phrase "in the subject (*pakṣe*)"—meaning in the earth and so forth—is to be supplied.
The sense is that the fact that the earth and other things are effects is established by their possessing form (*ākṛtimattva*) and other such properties.

In order to demonstrate that the specific nature of the agent is established by the force of the property of being a predicate (pakṣadharmatā), he determines the general nature of the effect and its material cause with the word "here" (iha). The meaning is as follows: "final part-wholeness" (antyāvayavitva) is the state of being a whole that is not co-referential with the state of being a part.

Starting from final wholes and extending back to the first whole, the dyad (dyaṇuka), it is well known that the entire class of composite effect-substances is produced by a particular conjunction of parts.
The term "gradually diminishing" (*kramanihīyamāna*) refers to the decrease in the number of constituent parts (*avayava*) in each preceding effect relative to its successor.

Furthermore, the fact that [the size of the effect] is produced by a specific conjunction of parts is established in some cases through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and in others through inference (*anumāna*). This is the intended meaning.
"Being the final substrate" (*antyopādānatva*) means being a part (*avayava*) that does not reside in the same locus as the state of being a whole (*avayavitva*).
There are four kinds of atoms: the atoms of earth, water, fire, and air.
Regarding the phrase "of them," it refers to the manifold of effects, that is, the manifold of derivative substances (*kāryadravya*).

The initial motion of atoms—characterized as the action that produces the productive conjunction at the time of the beginning of creation—is caused by a non-inherent cause consisting of the conjunction of the self with the unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*); this is the meaning of the "instrumentality" of the unseen forces.

Furthermore, the fact that the first motion is caused by the unseen force was formulated as a sutra by the sage Kaṇāda: "The upward flaming of fire, the horizontal blowing of wind, and the first actions of atoms and of the mind are brought about by the unseen force.
This is the "purpose."

The purpose of creation is the assistance of living beings (*jīva*), which is infinite and consists of an incalculable variety of types of assistance; its nature is the performance of various kinds of purposeful actions (*arthakriyā*) carried out by the created objects, characterized by the production of manifold enjoyments. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the recipients (*sampradāna*) are the multitudes of living beings who experience the enjoyment produced by the effected objects, whether directly or indirectly; thus he says, "those who enjoy that."

Thus, by the logic of *kaimutika* (how much more so), he states "And these [souls] do not [perceive]" in order to establish that even the capacity to directly perceive one's own *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit) does not belong to them, let alone the capacity to directly perceive all kinds of atoms, all living beings, all types of unseen forces, all modes of assistance to every living being, and the entire world in its form as material cause, instruments, and purposes.
That which is distinct from that—distinct from the individual soul—is the *adhikaraṇasiddhānta*.

The Nyāya Sūtra states: "That is an *adhikaraṇasiddhānta* by the establishment of which there is the establishment of another matter. Without the establishment of which the subject at hand cannot be established.

The meaning is that an object which is established as being inseparable from the establishment of the subject matter at hand (*prakṛtārtha*) is established by way of a "presumption based on the context" (*adhikaraṇasiddhānta*). Thus, since the nature of the earth and other things having an agent cannot be established unless there is the direct perception of all objects and so forth, it follows that the attainment of a specific agent occurs according to the principle of *adhikaraṇasiddhānta*.
The Mīmāṃsakas refute this method of inferring God (Īśvara) favored by the logicians (Tārkikas) with the words "This very [inference]," and so forth.

The meaning is that this proof for a unique person (the Lord)—which is rooted in fallacious reasoning (tarkābhāsa) devised by their own intellects and lacks systematic consistency—is based on the principle that inference establishes only that which is of a similar class to what has been perceived, and not an object beyond the senses; thus, it arises from one who does not understand the actual operation of inference.
The phrase "the designation of one who is ignorant of the nature of reasoning as a logician is most striking" contains an implicit mockery.
He begins to demonstrate the fallacious nature of the reasoning stated by the opponent with the words "for instance" (*tathāhi*).
Then he asks: "What is this? (*kimidam*)?
"Of the microcosm and the macrocosm," such as the individual body and the cosmic egg;
"piṇḍa" means the body.
Thus it is said in the *Purāṇaratna*: "The *piṇḍa* is that which is distinct from the Person (puṃs), characterized by the head, hands, and so forth."
Or, the meaning may be "in the case of the subject and the similar instance.
Having proposed that the world is dependent on a single conscious being, he refutes this with the verse beginning "Is this... (*kimasya*).
"Dependent" (*āyatta*) means connected by way of being its effect (*kāryatvena*).
Is it being caused by a single volition that is being proven regarding the origin of the world, or its maintenance, or rather its activity?
The meaning is that in the first two alternatives, the concordant example (anvaya-dṛṣṭānta) of a healthy body is deficient in the probandum (sādhyavikala).
Thus, the implication is that there is both a failure to establish pervasion (vyāptyasiddhi) and a deviation (vyabhicāra). // 6 //

If you aim merely to prove that [the world] is dependent upon volition (*cetanā*), you are proving what is already established for us; for we maintain that the objects of experience are produced by karmas, which are themselves experienced by sentient beings who are the enjoyers. (7)
And this is logical: that one should accept the agency of only those conscious beings that are established for both disputants, on account of parsimony (*lāghava*).
Nor can there be a rejection of that [agency] on the grounds of their being ignorant of the material cause (*upādāna*) and so forth.
He demonstrates the absence of the probandum (*sādhyavikalatva*) in the example with the words beginning "Indeed, not... (*na khalu...*) and so on.
It must be stated that even for one's own body, its production and maintenance have as their cause [the self] by way of its own *adṛṣṭa* (unseen moral force).

Furthermore, for others who partake in the assistance of enjoyment dependent upon that body, there exists a causality by way of *adṛṣṭa* just as there is for the possessor of that body; thus, the meaning is that in the example, the state of having production and maintenance dependent on a single conscious being does not exist.
Regarding the second alternative, he states another refutation by means of analyzing the meaning of the word "maintenance" (*sthiti*), beginning with "Moreover" (*api ca*).
The term *śarīrāvayavinaḥ* is a *karmadhāraya* compound.

When the originating conjunction (*ārambhaka-saṃyoga*), which inheres in the parts, is firm, the stability of the whole (*avayavin*)— characterized by its inherence in its own parts— is established without obstruction for the body, just as it is well-known for a jar or similar objects.
Such a state of stability does not depend upon consciousness.

While the maintenance of the body—characterized by its persistence in a state of non-laxity dependent on the vital functions (*prāṇavṛtti*)—might indeed depend upon consciousness because it is caused by the effort that is the source of life (*jīvanayoni*), such dependence is certainly established as a pervading property in the example; however, this kind of stability does not exist in the subject (*pakṣa*), such as the earth and so forth.

And thus, the point is that if one were to prove, by means of the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*), that things have their existence dependent upon a single such conscious agent, there would be partial sublation (*aṃśato bādha*).

Regarding the third alternative—that [the world] has its activity dependent on a single conscious agent—he states the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) with the word "eke" (some). "Sarabhasaprayatnaḥ" means intense effort.

The meaning is that the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because it exists in a great stone and the like, which are devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhya*), yet possess the activity of movement that can be accomplished by many people.
Furthermore, he states that the qualification of the reason is superfluous with the words "precisely because it has been begun.
If "being produced" (*janyatva*) alone were the reason, no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) would be possible; therefore, the qualification "being determined by an insentient material cause" is redundant.
And thus, there is the fallacy of the unestablished nature of the pervasion (vyāpyatvāsiddhi).
The intention is that they employ "the superfluous" (adhika) as a point of defeat (nigrahasthāna).
Although, when the reason is refined into the form of "being a substance inherent [in its cause]," the contingency of futility (vaiyarthya) does not arise.

Furthermore, even if one were to argue that the qualification is superfluous based on the intended meaning of the reason as it was originally heard, the fact remains that once the reason has established its conclusion, the charge of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) is indeed unavoidable; this is the general direction of the argument. Now, one might object: "The qualification of 'oneness' (*ekatva*) is abandoned because it leads to the contingency of inconclusiveness."
If it is argued that what is being proven is simply the state of being dependent on volition (*cetanā*), he says "volition" (*cetana*) in response.
Although for one who speaks thus, the aforementioned fallacies such as the abandonment of the thesis (*uktahāni*) and so forth certainly follow,
nevertheless, because those are faults of the formulation, they are here disregarded and only the refutation of the actual meaning is stated.
The word "hi" signifies a well-known fact.

Since we also agree that the commonality of effects (kāryasāmānya) depends upon consciousness because it has the unseen merit of living beings (jīvādṛṣṭa) as its cause, if you are merely proving dependence on consciousness, you are proving what is already established for us by means of living beings; furthermore, for you, it would result in proving something other than your intended point. This is the sense. //7//
The material substrates, such as earth and so forth, as well as the means of sacrifice and giving, are all capable of being directly perceived by every conscious being. (8)

Up until now, the earth and other elements possess only partial increases and decreases of adventitious qualities acquired through karma; they do not simultaneously undergo total destruction and creation. Therefore, the direct perception of the final atom is not conducive to the status of being an agent.
[Objection: But if it is mediated by *adṛṣṭa*, then mere non-dependence [on such a cause] is not what is being proven.
But if it is argued that [the world] must have an intelligent agent as its creator, and that such agency is not possible for individual souls (jīvas) with respect to the earth and so forth;
if this is the case, then the conclusion rests solely upon the second inference.
To the objection that even in that case it would be a mere proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), he says "it is not logical" (*ayuktam*).
The intention is that because inference favors parsimony (*lāghava*), the inference of having an agent—even for the world—rests solely upon the well-known individual soul (*jīva*).
[Objection: But surely, it is untenable for the individual soul to be the creator of the universe.
He rejects the doubt that "if the object [of creation] were impossible, then parsimony would be irrelevant,
and thus the proof of God would be unimpeded" with the words "nor in the material cause.
He states "the material cause" to show that even for the individual soul (jīva), the direct perception of the material cause and so forth is indeed possible.

This is the intended meaning: having understood from the Veda and from the words of the Vedists that each specific Vedic rite is the means for attaining its respective superior fruit, and having performed those various rites according to rule through the very grace of those [scriptures], certain individual souls who have acquired a particular capacity [take] the four elements— earth and the rest— which constitute the material cause (*upādāna*) of the class of elemental effects, as well as the class of auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*).

And since they would create the world by means of direct perception and material causes, there is no room for postulating another creator; because they are capable [of this], there is no rejection of that [position]—this is the syntactical connection with what precedes. // 8 //
Let it be that the form of the power of karma, which is the referent of terms such as *apūrva*, is not perceptible; however, the possessor of that power is within the range of perception.

Indeed, potters and others, when beginning an effect such as a jar, do not undertake it after having directly perceived the capacity of the clay, staff, wheel, and other implements—which serve as its material and instrumental causes—to produce that specific effect.
At most, for those unaware of such a capacity, the practical engagement with the material causes and so forth toward the accomplishment of a desired object would be untenable;

however, in this case—surely, at the time of dissolution (pralaya), because the primary dyads (dvyaṇuka) of earth and the rest have perished, and because living beings at that time are devoid of the excellence of their instruments (karaṇa)—[the Lord’s knowledge of capacities is required].
To the objection that the agency of those [elements] in the creation of the world at the beginning of a cycle is impossible due to their lack of the capacity to take up knowledge, he says: "As now.
There is no dissolution or production of the earth and other elements in their entirety;
rather, like in the present time, these two occur sequentially only through a division of parts.
These two [processes] are characterized by the increase and decrease of adventitious portions.

Thus, even among living beings, for certain individuals who have attained a preeminent power of knowledge through specific means, creation—in the form of filling out deficient parts—can indeed occur based on the direct perception of material causes such as the earth, just as in the case of Viśvāmitra and others; this is the meaning.
In a dissolution without remainder (*niravaśeṣapralaya*), there is no further creation.

However, in a dissolution with remainder (*sāvaśeṣalaya*), it is possible for specific individual souls (*jīva*) to act as the agents of differentiation for their respective portions; thus, the point is that there is no occasion for postulating a Lord (*īśvara*).
[Objection: But surely there is also the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*)—consisting of merit and demerit—as a cooperative cause.
And if there were direct realization of that [Brahman], the creation of effects conforming to it would not be possible;
furthermore, such direct realization is not feasible for individual souls (jīvas). To this, he says: "Of action" (karmaṇaḥ).
This refers to the direct realization of dharmas such as sacrifices performed by others, as well as adharma such as theft and the like.
Patience itself is the witness to these specific types of living beings;
moreover, through the sacred teachings, they have understood the capacity of various actions to produce their respective specific fruits,
and thus they may indeed create accordingly.

The direct realization of the possessor of power (śaktimat) and the mere cognition of power (śakti) are what contribute to agency, but the direct realization of power itself is not required. Furthermore, as for oneself...
And the capacity of the instrument is required;
thus, even when there is no direct perception of the power of karma—termed merit and demerit—there is no obstruction to the existence of an agent. This is the intended meaning. // 9 //
The diverse potencies of karma are understood from scripture;
therefore, let individual selves fashion themselves separately by means of their respective karmas.

Furthermore, in this world, only that which is capable of being produced and for which the material causes and so forth are capable of being known is observed to have an intelligent agent as its creator.
Since this is not the case with the earth, mountains, great oceans, and so forth, how can they possibly be considered effects?
And how can that [material cause], its instruments, and so forth, fall within the range of direct perception?

For only such an effect as is known to be preceded by one who is cognizant of its material cause and so forth— such as a jar or a water-pot— is capable of serving as the basis for inferring a cause possessed of such an intelligent intellect.

Furthermore, since a product such as a jar is understood to have been made by one who is non-omnipotent, possessed of limited power and knowledge, embodied, and one whose desires are not yet fulfilled,

a logical reason (*hetu*) that posits such a cognizer would be contradictory (*viruddha*), as it establishes the opposite of the intended person’s omniscience, omnipotence, and so forth. Nor, this being the case, should one fear the consequence of the total collapse of all inferential practice.

For when the subject possessing the mark (liṅgin) falls within the scope of another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), that very cognition prevents the contrary particulars that would otherwise follow by the force of the mark. Here, however, when that which is skilled in all emanations— which transcends the operation of all other means of valid cognition— is what is sought to be proven, it presents without distinction even all those properties that possess an invariable concomitance (avinābhāva) as determined through positive and negative pervasion (anvaya-vyatireka).
He establishes this very point by way of an illustration with the word "not" (na).
This [particle] is employed in the sense of the word "but" (tu),
or rather, it means "prior to this," namely, prior to the word "here" (iha).
The word "satyam" (it is true) is to be supplied. Regarding the phrase "from scripture":
this means through the understanding, based on the scriptures, of the powers residing in ritual action.
By means of actions— that is, due to the causes of the actions of various living beings,
which is to say, in accordance with their karma— the selves, meaning the sentient beings who possess power.
By means of distinct divisions— that is, through the differentiation of each respective part—
the entire world, consisting of all classes of produced substances.
"nirmimatām" means "let them create. // 10 //
Moreover: The actions of a discerning being are pervaded by either self-interest or compassion;
since both are absent in the case of Īśvara, the creation of the world is not tenable. (11)
Since his desires have been fulfilled, he does not create for his own sake;

and at the time of dissolution, because all instruments of experience such as bodies and sense organs have dissolved, sentient beings lack suffering. Thus, there is no impetus of compassion arising from the sight of those who suffer.
Consequently, since both the pervasive factors—self-interest and compassion—have ceased, the subordinate factor—purposeful activity by a rational agent—must also necessarily cease.
Now, he states the defects in the reason "being an effect" with the words beginning "Moreover" (*api ca*).

Therein, first, the unestablished nature of the essential character (*svarūpāsiddhi*) and the unestablished nature of the pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*) by way of a limiting condition (*upādhi*) are proclaimed.
That which can be produced—that is, that for which an action (*kriyā*) or instrument (*karaṇa*) is possible—is "capable of being produced" (*śakyakraya*).
"Capable of being produced" means that which can be made.

"Capable of being known" refers to knowledge that is possible; "having a capable-of-being-known material cause and so forth" refers to an effect whose material cause and other factors are such that they can be known.

The meaning is that an effect of such a nature must necessarily have an agent; this is because one should consider that there is no effect devoid of an intelligent agent. Thus [it says] "And not... etc.

"Tattatkāryatvam" means the state of being the effect of this or that [cause], such as the earth and so forth, which are impossible to produce; by this, he states either a failure to establish the essential nature (*svarūpāsiddhi*) or a partial failure to establish it (*bhāgāsiddhi*). "How else? [is the question].

The meaning is as follows: since it is impossible to directly perceive the material causes, instruments, atoms, unseen forces (*adṛṣṭa*), and so forth [of the earth], how could it possibly be established that things such as the earth and the binary atomic compounds (*dvyaṇuka*) are preceded by a person who possesses the desire to perceive those material causes and the like, as well as the volition and action [to produce them]?

If there is a persistent insistence on the fact that the earth and other such things are effects, then let it be accepted; however, the point is that their being produced by an agent (*sakartṛkatva*) is indeed logically consistent.
He states that [the property] has a limiting adjunct (*sopādhikatva*) with the words "of such a kind" (*yādṛśam*).
"Of such a kind" means [that which is] fit to be accomplished by volitional effort (*kṛti-sādhyatvārha*) and fit to have its material cause and so forth known (*jñeyatvārha-upādānādika*).
By this, it is stated that the limiting adjunct consists in being capable of being produced and having its material cause and so forth capable of being known.
Its nature as a sublater through deviation (*vyabhicāra*) or as a sublater of a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*) should be understood.

Having thus stated that the reason of "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) does not prove that it is preceded by an intended agent, he states that it leads to an unintended consequence with the words "Moreover" (*api ca*).

For in the case of the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), such as a pot, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of "being an effect" has been apprehended as being preceded by an agent characterized by having a body, dependence on his own purposes, and non-omnipotence.
Furthermore, the body and so forth, which have their pervasion (*vyāpti*) grasped with respect to a specific probandum (*sādhya*), would prove only a specific agent in the subject (*pakṣa*).
Since those features (*ākāra*) are the opposite of what is intended, the reason is "contradictory" (*viruddha*) because it is pervaded by the contradictory. This is the sense.

[Objection: But in that case, in a similar instance (*sapakṣa*) such as a kitchen, smoke whose pervasion has been grasped with fire possessing qualities like being produced from cow-dung (*kārīṣatva*) would result in proving only fire of that very kind—such as that produced from cow-dung—in the subject, the mountain.
And since that [specificity] does not exist there, it follows that inference as a whole would lack validity; to this he says, "But it is not so.
Regarding the phrase "by another means of knowledge":

when the probandum is apprehended by another means of knowledge, the contradictory particulars that might follow from the force of the logical mark (*liṅga*) are sublated by perception and other means; thus, the validity of inference is established only with respect to fire in general.

The intention is as follows: when the probandum (sādhya) lies beyond the scope of other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), there would be no sublater (apavādaka) for those contrary particulars that follow from the force of the logical mark (liṅga); thus, they would remain exactly as they are.

For instance, when the pervasion (vyāpti) of "being an effect" by "having an agent delimited by specific attributes" is grasped through the apprehension of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka-sahacāra), those attributes—such as being a potter, non-omnipotence, and being subject to saṃsāra—which are inherent in such agents, are grasped as the delimiters of the pervader (vyāpakatāvacchedaka).

Furthermore, because the nature of a logical mark (*liṅga*) is to lead to the inference of a probandum (*sādhya*) by way of its delimiting property (*vyāpakatāvacchedakadharma*), the inference of "having an agent" based on the reason of "being an effect" necessarily results in [an agent who is] merely a non-divine transmigrating being; this is what is intended by the phrase "as many as... and so forth.

Intending to show that the aforementioned inference rests upon none other than a non-divine agent—since it is impossible for God (*Īśvara*) to be the creator of the world—he says, "And if not... (*apace*).
"Self-interest" (*svārtha*) means one's own purpose.
"Compassion" (*kāruṇya*) is a specific quality conducive to accomplishing the purpose of others, which is synonymous with altruism (*parārtha*).
The meaning of the first half-verse is that the general property of intelligent activity is pervaded by the mere existence of either the desire for one's own interest or compassion.

However, in the case of God, who is intended to be proven as the creator, no motive for creation can exist that serves His own interest, because He has already attained all desires; nor can compassion be the cause,
since that arises from the perception of others' suffering, and at the time of dissolution, there is an absolute absence of suffering among others.

Therefore, the meaning of the second half [of the verse] is that there is a cessation of the activity consisting in the creation of the world, due to the cessation of its pervader—namely, either the intention for one's own benefit or the awakening of compassion. // 11 //
If he were to produce a world uniformly oriented toward happiness by means of compassion,
then his sovereignty would be lost, given that [the world] conforms to its own past karma.

Nor is there a rule that agency belongs only to one who directly perceives the instruments of action (upādāna) and so forth; for even a self ignorant of the instruments and accessories possesses agency in acts such as cognition. He elaborates the meaning of the verse with the words beginning "avāpti" (attainment), etc.
He states the impossibility of compassion in another way with the half-verse beginning "sukhaika-":
the point is that, on the contrary, not even a trace of compassion is compatible for one who creates a world that is an abode of suffering.
[Objection: But surely the Lord engages in creation out of compassion alone?
Furthermore, regarding the objection that there is no consequence of cruelty and so forth because creation depends upon the karma of those to be created, he says: "That karma.
The sense is that if that were the case, the consequence of dependence on karma would follow, and thus his status as the Lord (Īśvara) would be lost.
Here, one should consider the counter-argument (*pratitarka*): if the Lord were the creator of the world, he would possess such qualities as not having all his desires fulfilled.
The counter-application, however, will indeed be explained further on. // 12 //

Therefore—due to the reasons already described, namely that the probans "being an effect" is unestablished, contradictory, and inconclusive—the world does not have an agent as previously asserted. (13)

And the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: the earth, mountains, and so forth do not constitute an effect [produced by a conscious agent], because they are dissimilar to well-known effects, like space; or else, because their material causes and instruments are impossible to perceive.
[The argument] by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is as follows:
atoms are not perceptible because they are substances of unsurpassed subtlety, just like jars and the like;
this is the subject of dispute.
Time is not devoid of a world,
because it is time, just like the present time.
The body, the world, and so forth do not have God as their creator, because they are effects, just like that [present time].
"God is not an agent because he lacks a purpose, or because he is bodiless, like a liberated soul.

Furthermore, [the opponent] states the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) regarding the proof that [the world] must be preceded by an agent who knows the material cause and so forth, saying: "And not the material cause, etc.

Since the self is perceptible only through the coloring of specific qualities such as knowledge, at the time of engaging in an action for the sake of knowledge, the self does not necessarily possess the direct intuition of its own self, which is the material cause of that knowledge.
Nor is there the status of being a direct agent (*sākṣātkartṛtva*) with respect to the mind (*manas*) and so forth, which are the instruments for that [cognition].
Since activity is directed toward knowledge, the agency in knowledge consists merely in being the inherent cause (*samavāyitva*).

Thus, the meaning is that there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*), because the property of having the same effect as knowledge exists even in that which lacks being preceded by the knowledge of the material cause and so forth.
The refutations of the arguments for a creator based on etymology and inference are summarized by the phrase "because of being unestablished" (*asiddhatvāt*).

The property of being an effect (*kāryatva*) is unestablished in respect to the earth and so forth, because the inference that [the earth] is not an effect—due to its being impossible to produce and so on—subverts the contrary characteristics such as non-creatorship, non-attainment of desires, and possession of a body; thus, the property of being an effect, which is intended to be proven as belonging to the agent of the earth and so forth, is contradictory (*viruddha*).
For it is the traditional definition of the ancients that the "contradictory" nature (*viruddhatva*) of a reason consists in its implying a form contrary to what is intended.

Furthermore, the fact that [the reason] entails a lack of sovereignty and so forth follows precisely because the probans of "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) has been apprehended in things such as jars as being pervaded by "having an agent characterized by a lack of sovereignty" and so on.

Moreover, if the probandum were merely "being produced by a conscious being," there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), since it is accepted that in all effects whatsoever, production by a living being occurs through the medium of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*).
Therefore, one must accept that the probandum (sādhya) is "having a creator who directly perceives the material cause and so forth.
In this regard, the inconclusiveness (anaikāntya) mentioned immediately above remains established due to the inclusion of [entities such as] knowledge and the like.

Thus, because the property of being an effect (kāryatva) is vitiated by defects such as being unestablished (asiddhi), it cannot prove that the earth and other things are preceded by a creator who directly perceives the material cause, instruments, and so forth; this is the meaning. // 13 //

To this we reply: it is not possible to deny that earth and the other elements possess the nature of being effects, because they possess commonality, because they possess activity, and because they are qualified by magnitude. (14)

Precisely because it possesses such corporeality, is endowed with external perceptibility, and consists of both general and particular characteristics, [the self] is [inferred] like a jar and other such objects. (15)
We do not observe a specific difference in form restricted to a particular arrangement of parts, such that "only this kind of arrangement must be produced and no other.
As for the fact that something is produced which is capable of being made and whose materials and instruments are capable of being known— let that indeed be so.
However, those two powers— of action and knowledge— are to be attained through action and knowledge alone;

and since these are established in the earth and other elements by the force of the aforementioned means, there is no distinction between the body and the world on one hand, and well-known effects such as walls and gate-towers on the other.
Nor is there any observed restriction regarding the scope of action such that the domain of action is limited to this much alone,
by which we might determine that this [universe] is something impossible to create.

And once its status as an effect is established, a specific Person who is skilled in the direct perception of its material cause and so forth, its supervision, and its impulsion, is indeed established.
And that "presiding" (adhiṣṭhāna) is the proximity of the Lord, who possesses a volition conducive to its [the body's] activity,
just as the knower of the field [the soul] is [proximate] to his own body and so forth;
and that [proximity], in the case of substances, is characterized by conjunction (saṃyoga).
It consists of an inherent conjunction (*samavāya*) with those qualities.
Furthermore, the activity (*pravṛtti*) of atoms is characterized by vibration;

whereas for merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), it is the state of being accompanied by such auxiliary causes (*sahakārī*) as place, time, and so forth, which are conducive to the arising of their results.
The fruit arises from those two alone, merit and demerit,
because all these [other factors], being insentient, are incapable of acting when not presided over by volition; for indeed,
an axe is not effective when not wielded by a conscious carpenter.
Even when a hundred auxiliary conditions such as place and time are present, they are capable of producing [artifacts] like sacrificial posts;

however, since seeds, sprouts, and the like are included within the subject of the argument (*pakṣa*), the claim that there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) by means of them is simply due to the ignorance of the Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*).
By this, the charge of deviation by means of pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth is also refuted.

Nor is it appropriate to postulate that the individual souls (kṣetrajñas) alone possess such a capacity for presiding over [the world] merely because they are established by both parties; for it is certain that they lack the power to perceive subtle, concealed, and other such objects.
Indeed, in all cases, a postulation must follow what is observed.
It is not contradicted by perception;
nor is the incapacity of the Lord thus established,
because that [capacity] is proven by other means of valid cognition.
Established by the force of the aforementioned means of valid cognition, it is proven that [the Creator] is endowed with the innate vision of all objects and the power to impel them;
for there is an invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*) between the state of being an effect and its being preceded by a capable agent.

As for the objection raised—that [the argument] proves the opposite of the specific property (*dharmaviśeṣa*) because it results in [the attribution of] limited power, knowledge, and lack of sovereignty—[this is not the case].
Therefore, that [objection] stands refuted, because those [causes] lack causal efficacy;
for nothing being produced depends, upon its own arising, on the incapacity or ignorance of the agent regarding some other object.
Because the mere agent capable of producing its own effect is implied [by the existence of the effect], a purely negative concomitance (*kevalavyatireka*) is not established;

for when the arising of the effect is accounted for by that much alone, it is illogical to postulate as a cause the absence of a related entity—which is itself non-productive and concerns a different object.
Furthermore, what is that "other" which is a real entity?
It must be discerned whether this knowledge of the self and so forth is all-pervasive or has only a limited scope;
it cannot, first of all, have everything as its object.
Because of non-apprehension.
Indeed, it is not the case that the potter does not know anything at all beyond the pot; rather, he knows only a limited range of objects.
That too is not the case, because since its object is not fixed, it is observed to deviate from this or that [subject].
Nor is there anything established such that only one who possesses ignorance and so forth experiences agency.
Nor must it be the case that the agent is necessarily embodied,
for there is an inconclusiveness (anaikāntya) due to the very fact of taking up a body;
indeed, this self does not take up a body while already being distinguished by a body.
For it is impossible for one who is not a yogi to simultaneously assume multiple bodies.

It has been established in the *Ātmacintā* that, by abandoning its previous body, the self enters another body only with the assistance of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is impelled by karma that brings about the acquisition of a new body. Furthermore, when the self presides over a body, the state of the presiding agent (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*) [is distinct from] the body, which is the object of the action of presiding (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
[Such] entry is untenable,
because it is contradictory for a single entity to be both the object and the agent of the same simultaneous action.

If it is argued that presiding (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is observed to be characterized by the possession of an effort conducive to that activity, [only] in one who possesses a conjunction with a body intended to be presided over;
Let it be that [the argument] "because superintendence is impossible for one connected with a single principle (sattva), there must be a prompter related to the object to be prompted" holds;
however, this is not [an argument] based on a connection with the body.
"It must be cultivated"—
from what source is this determination derived?

Precisely from this very point, because even other things being presided over, such as the body and so forth produced by the means of valid cognition (*māna*), are presided over by their own respective correlates.

Therefore, one should not regard the connection with a body as something distinct from the mere relationship between the object to be empowered and the act of empowerment required for that purpose; indeed, it has already been stated that even the Lord possesses a connection with the material causes and instruments of the universe.
Furthermore, his engagement with objects distinct from his own body occurs precisely through the medium of a body.
It might be argued that the agency of a potter and others in setting a staff, wheel, and so forth in motion is indeed observed through the conjunction of their hands and other means;
yet even this is not so,
for we observe the expulsion and dispersal of poison residing in another's body by mere thought alone.
If it is asked, "How can there be a volition consisting of being impelled by another when the body does not exist?"— does the body itself will,
such that [volition] would not occur in its absence?
If it is argued that [the Lord] is an instrument (karaṇa), we say no;
for since the mind is an instrument, does the Lord possess a mind? Certainly he does.
But if this were so, then common attributes such as ignorance, attachment, merit, demerit, and lack of sovereignty would necessarily manifest in Him.
Not so; for [the argument] has already been refuted by the very strength of the fact that [the world] possesses a capable agent, which is implied by its being an effect.
Furthermore, [the reason] is inconclusive because the mind, being a permanent sense organ, is admitted to remain connected even upon the departure of the body.
For only that which conforms to what is observed and is useful for establishing a universal concomitance (vyāpti) is admitted;

and [this is not the case] regarding the manifold expansion of the primary elements and their derivatives, whose construction is inconceivable even by the mind of one such as us and whose extent is limitless.

If it is argued that the connection between "being an effect" and a creator such as this has not been observed in the case of jars and other things— [whereas] a limited-bodied being, one who knows only a little, whose movement is subject to merit and demerit, is quite incapable of creation; whereas [the true creator] possesses immeasurable power of knowledge and sovereignty, is independent of the body and so forth, and is established as the agent capable of creating the entire universe through mere volition alone.

Has the connection of smoke with a particular fire been observed in a kitchen or similar place— a fire characterized by its location on the exceedingly deep mountain slope and its association with a vast,
previously unseen mass of fuel— such that, upon seeing a particular kind of smoke, a fire of that same nature could be inferred on a mountain peak?

For it is only when a smoke of a certain kind is known to exist in a specific place that such a smoke, even if not perceived in the instance serving as the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), is established by the force of universal concomitance (*sāmānyavyāpti*) through its presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).
If this is so, why does this which we are stating not take root in your hearts?

Even this property of being an effect, whose necessary connection with a capable agent has been established in the case of jars and the like, when observed in the case of the earth and other such things, brings to mind an intelligent agent capable of producing it, even though such an agent has never been seen before.
For just as there is a necessary connection of smoke with fire in general— without regard for specific differences such as place, time, or the quantity of fuel— so too,
by setting aside specific attributes such as non-omnipotence, lack of omniscience, corporeality, subjection to merit and demerit, and human nature,

there is a determination of a necessary connection between an effect and an intelligent agent in general who possesses the capacity for its creation; thus, there is no difference whatsoever [between the two cases].

Moreover, although there is no deviation from the rule that everything conjoined with an all-pervading substance or possessing motion possesses touch, how can the mind— which is conjoined with the self as inferred from its specific qualities such as cognition, pleasure, and so forth— be devoid of touch? Or, why is it that the tactile organ exhibits the opposite, despite the observed rule that a substance composed of air, which possesses the quality of magnitude, has a fixed location and is characterized by tangibility?

Even if there were a rule regarding the manifestation of either color or touch in that which is fiery (*taijasa*), one must nevertheless accept that in the case of the eye—which is inferred to be fiery because it is the means for perceiving color—there is invariably a non-manifestation of both those qualities.

Furthermore, although their existence is inferred from the observation of their effects, even if they are of a fiery nature, the specific qualities [of fire] are sublated by the non-perception of what is otherwise perceptible (*yogyānupalabdhi*); moreover, to accept them would entail the collapse of numerous established rules.

Well then, since there is no difference in the sublation by non-perception regarding the specific properties acquired through practice even in the case of innate dispositions (*prakṛti*), and because it would follow that the observation of various constraints would be undermined, such an admission [of the possibility of change] applies equally to both cases, except for your dogmatic attachment. For indeed, political strategies (*nīti*) are observed [to change].
Just as the subject of dispute, such as atoms and so forth, acts impelled by a conscious being,
because it is insentient; whatever is insentient acts in that manner.
Just as such things as a ball [are preceded by direct perception],
so too the external and internal activities under dispute are preceded by the direct perception of their material causes and instruments, because they are effects, exactly like that [ball].
He states the formal argument (*prayoga*) with the words "And the formal argument."
He establishes that [the world] has an imperceptible material cause by stating "atoms. In this very way— that is, through the method of exclusion alone—
the formal argument (prayoga) has been stated to prove the non-establishment of the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*) in the subject (*pakṣa*), namely the earth and so forth.

Now, in order to establish that [the argument] is already proven by the existence of living beings (*jīva*), the formal argument (*prayoga*) for refuting dissolution (*pralaya*) is stated as "vimati" (disagreement).

For if dissolution were to exist, then at the commencement of creation, the status of being a creator could not belong to the living beings because they are devoid of instruments and the like; thus, another agent would have to be postulated.
Therefore, it is here established that dissolution—characterized by the total absence of all effect-substances—does not exist at all.
The formal argument (*prayoga*) beginning with "the body, mountains, forests, etc. is intended to demonstrate contradiction (*viruddhatva*).
The phrase "it does not have God as its agent" results in the meaning that "it has a non-God agent.
In the same way, by positive concomitance (*anvaya*), it is like a jar and so forth.
It has been stated that the inference from the nature of being an effect results in a contrary conclusion;
and it clarifies its lack of the intended conclusion with the word "Īśvara.
Here, "Īśvara" refers to one who is regarded as being Īśvara.
And this [reason] takes the form of a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*).
