Thus, having relied upon the very method of the logicians (*tārkika*), the Mīmāṃsakas begin to attempt to establish the inference for God (*īśvarānumāna*)—which they have indeed already criticized—by way of removing its defects, starting with the words "In this regard, we say," and so forth;
[here] "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) means "having an origin" (*utpattimattva*).
The reasons for the earth and so forth being effects are their having commonality (*sabhāgatva*) and other such qualities.
"Having commonality" means "having parts" (*sāvayavatva*).
As for the reading *vittyādibhyaḥ* found in older printed editions, it is not correct.

Since the possession of activity (*kriyāvattva*) and corporeality (*mūrtatva*), which consists in having a delimited dimension (*paricchinnaparimāṇavattva*), are common to eternal atoms (*nityaparamāṇu*), they are made the cause [of the inference] by being qualified by largeness (*mahattva*) through the relation of co-inherence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
The general and particular properties (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*) are [the universals] such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) and so forth, and [the particulars] such as earthness (*pṛthivītva*) and so forth.
Since that [property] alone is common to eternal atoms (*paramāṇu*) and so forth, it was specified as being the object of external perception and made the reason for the argument. [Objection:

Because the self (*ātman*) is an object of mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*) and possesses both generality (*sāmānya*) and particularity (*viśeṣa*), there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in that case; therefore, perception is specified by the qualification "external" (*bāhya*). // 14 // 15 //
That [self] is perceptible because it is an object of knowledge and because it is a category of existence, like a jar and so forth;
this [body] follows the will of another because it is insentient, like one's own body. (16)

But surely, let there be "being an effect" by virtue of the aforementioned reasons; what follows from that regarding "having an agent"? For there is a lack of evidence that an agent is the cause of "effect-ness" in general.
To the objection that the production of the earth and so forth is possible even without an agent due to other causes, he says: "And not such [a thing].
For "having parts" (sāvayavatva) means possessing a form consisting of a specific arrangement of parts;
and since that is observed to be achievable only through human effort, it must be admitted that even the earth and other things with diverse forms possess an agent.
Let it be that the state of being a specific kind of effect (*kāryaviśeṣatva*) alone is pervaded by having an agent (*sakartṛkatvavyāpya*).
And since that specific quality is not excluded from the earth and so forth, the proof of their having an agent remains unimpeded.

Furthermore, according to the maxim "whatever [is the cause] of two specific [effects]," because the potter and others are the causes of a specific effect, [the property of having an agent] applies even to that which is merely delimited by the nature of being an effect (*kāryatvāvacchinna*).

The point is that since causality indeed belongs to that which is delimited by agency (*kartṛtva*), it is precisely the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*) that, as a pervader of having an agent (*sakartṛkatva*), establishes an agent in the case of the earth and so forth.

Alternatively, regarding the argument "the earth and so forth are not effects because they differ from well-known effects," he states "not such" (*na cedṛśa*) to show that this [reason] is non-conclusive (*aprayojaka*).
An "effect" (*kārya*) is that which is produced by volitional effort (*kṛti*).

The meaning is that we do not perceive any specific property— distinct from the form of the earth and other such things— that resides solely in the form of a jar and the like, which would serve as the probans (prayojaka) for its being produced by an agent.
For if such a specific property existed, then the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the difference from well-known effects and the state of being produced by a non-agent or an agent would be established.

Otherwise, however, the reason would be simply non-conclusive (*aprayojaka*), just as in the argument: "The royal palace has no unseen creator, because it is distinct from effects such as jars which have seen creators," and so forth—this is the sense.

If it is argued that a specific property such as "being capable of being produced" is precisely such a distinction that excludes the configuration of the earth and other things, he says in response: "As for that...
and "Let that be granted."
The underlying intention is that the absence of such a specific quality in earth and the other elements is unestablished (*asiddha*).
"Those two" refers to action and knowledge.
"As previously stated" means characterized by the inference of having an agent based on the reason of being an effect (*kāryatva*).

The intended meaning is as follows: what is to be proven regarding the earth and so forth is that they are produced by one who possesses direct knowledge, desire, and effort directed toward their material cause and other factors.
And in that case, the effort directed toward them, as well as the direct knowledge of their material cause and so forth, certainly exist as constituent elements.

The meaning is that since knowledge and action are thus established as authoritative, one must likewise postulate a capacity in the Creator of the world corresponding to them; therefore, [attributes such as] His inability to act and so forth are unproven. He is "established" (siddha) as one whose activity is the domain of volitional effort (kṛti).

The point is this: since being an effect is established as a valid property, and because the state of being an effect is invariably concomitant with being produced by a specific agent, the proof of a specific agent for the earth and so forth is indeed unimpeded.
The term "tadadhiṣṭhānatapreraṇe" is a *karmadhāraya* compound;
or alternatively, it refers to an activity conducive to the initiation of another's action.
The distinction is that *adhiṣṭhāna* (presiding) is the contact between the one possessing such activity and the object to be impelled.
Thus, the state of being an effect and, consequently, the state of having an agent for the earth and so forth have been established.

Now, in order to avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) by individual souls (*jīva*s) regarding the inference of having an agent (*sakartṛkatva*), he explains the presiding cause (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and so forth, which are inherent in the very nature of agency, with the words beginning "presiding" (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

The meaning is that just as a soul presides over the limbs and parts of a body through a volition conducive to their activity, so too must it be understood that the Lord, the creator of the world, presides over atoms, unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), and so forth, through a volition conducive to their activity.
Regarding the phrase "if that":

the contact with God (īśvara-sannikarṣa) in the case of atoms and the like is of the nature of conjunction (saṃyoga); and in the case of the unseen force (adṛṣṭa), it is of the nature of inherence in the conjoined (saṃyukta-samavāya), provided one accepts the conjunction of the two all-pervading substances.

If that [conjunction of the two all-pervading substances] is not accepted, it should be understood as being characterized by inherence in what is conjoined to the conjoined (saṃyukta-saṃyogi-samavāya).
And this is according to the method of the logicians (*tārkika*).
Regarding the term "activity" (*pravṛtti*): the meaning is that the activity of atoms consists of actions conducive to the conjunctions that initiate [the formation of composite bodies].
He explains the operation (*pravṛtti*) of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) with the words "of merit and demerit" (*dharmādharmayoḥ*).

The meaning is that the operation of the unseen force— which is rooted in the volition of the Lord (*īśvara-saṅkalpa*) that "may this merit or demerit produce its fruit in this particular place and at this particular time"—
consists in the acquisition of such auxiliary conditions (*sahakārī*) as the specific place, time, and so forth, which are conducive to the arising of the fruit.
Regarding the phrase "by those two":
the particle *eva* (only) is displaced [in the sentence].
The syntactical connection is: "the fruit [arises] only from those two, dharma and adharma, which are presided over by volition (*cetanā*)."
Indeed, harboring the doubt that the earth and so forth might arise from other causes even without a creator, he states the refutation with the words "conscious" (cetana).
He establishes the point that [other causes] are indeed ineffective with the words "for not" (na hi).

Thus, since there is a requirement for a conscious agent—a supervisor who employs the entire circle of causal factors—in the production of any effect in general, the fact that the earth and so forth possess a creator is not subject to denial.
The sense is that the activity of an insentient collection of causes is impossible without the superintendence of a sentient being.

Furthermore, since agency—defined as superintendence—is impossible without immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) whose object is the material cause and so forth, the creator of the earth and other things must necessarily possess direct perception of the atoms and other such factors. Moreover, impelling (*preraṇa*) is defined by an act of will (*kṛti*) which is the cause for setting in motion the circle of causal factors (*kārakacakra*) preceded by the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*); thus, it consists in being a superintendent whose nature is to employ the circle of causal factors, and whose characteristics are the possession of immediate knowledge, desire to act, and volition regarding the material cause and so forth.
Furthermore, there is no absolute difference between [the two types of] agency (*kartṛtva*).

Consequently, one should note that there is no room for the objection that "what was stated previously—namely, that agency consists in possessing immediate knowledge, desire to act, and volition directed toward the material cause and so forth—is here being established as having the nature of being a controller (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*), and thus the work of another [author] is inconsistent. This is what must be understood.

What is intended here is that since such agency over the earth and other elements is impossible for any being other than Īśvara—who is all-seeing and omnipotent—it is not a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) by those [opponents].
This will also be stated later in the subsequent text with the words "nor both proponents.
In the interim, he incidentally dispels the charge of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) with the word "in the seed" (*bīje*).
In every case where an agent is not observed,
all such effects are made the subject of the proposition (*pakṣa*);
and in the case of the subject, the suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) does not constitute a fault.
The meaning is that otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of the total abolition of the very discourse on inference (*anumāna*).
By the phrase "by this," the sense is: "precisely by being included within the subject (*pakṣa*)."
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), knowledge and so forth are to be understood.

For the living being (*jīva*), when engaged in activity for the sake of its own pleasure, knowledge, and so on, is not at that time the direct perceiver (*sākṣātkartṛ*) of its own self through the appropriation of those instruments.

Therefore, in the case of pleasure, knowledge, and so forth—which possess the probandum (*sādhya*) consisting in having as their antecedent a direct perceiver of that appropriation and so on—[the reason does not apply].

The argument that there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) because [the probans] "being an effect" (kāryatva) exists [in pleasure and so forth] is also refuted by including pleasure and the like within the subject (pakṣa) itself; this is the meaning.

The underlying intention is that even in those cases, the fact that [pleasure and so forth] are preceded by an agent who directly perceives their material cause and so on is established by us through the Lord (Īśvara) alone.
Now, one might object: "In that case, the individual soul (jīva) would not possess agency over its own pleasure and so forth. To this we reply: [it is not so].

This is because it is logically established by the very fact that there is an engagement in the acquisition and observation of means for the sake of accomplishing happiness and so forth— just as, for example, a potter engages with the acquisition and observation of visible tools and materials in the case of a jar.
However, it should be understood that the presiding over all effects, even those whose causes are unseen, belongs solely to the Supreme Self.

If it is argued that even so, since there is necessarily no direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of oneself at the time prior to the activity directed toward one's own cognition and so forth, the self does not possess the status of being the perceiver of its own self— which serves as the material cause (*upādāna*) for its own cognition— at that time; we say no, because according to the doctrine of the self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) of the self, the direct perception of one's own self must also be acknowledged at that very time.
Alternatively, there is no fault because one's own agency regarding one's own cognition and so forth must be admitted even on the basis of mere recollection of oneself.

Furthermore, it should not be forgotten that the rule—that [an effect] must be preceded by an agent who directly perceives the material cause and so on—is established by the Lord (Īśvara) himself in each respective case.
It should be understood that for this very purpose, pleasure and the like were also made the subject of the argument (*pakṣīkṛta*).
Having avoided the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), he avoids the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) with the words "nor both.
This means the postulation of a presiding agent who is conducive to the activity of atoms, the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), and so forth.
He states the reason for its being untenable with the words "of these."
The meaning is that for those who are unable even to perceive [the object], how can there be talk of its substratum?
Now, one might ask: "How can the unseen capacity of God to act as a substratum be postulated?
To this, he says: "And it is not so."
The meaning is that even what is not perceived does not contradict what is perceived.
Why is there no contradiction with perception? To this, he says: "by means of another pramāṇa."
Regarding this, it is doubted whether the reading should be "atadasiddheḥ" (because that is unestablished).
The meaning is that since God is not established by means such as perception, His incapacity has not been observed in Him.
To the objection that His incapacity will be established by this very inference, he says: "yathodite" (as stated).
But in the reading "tatsiddheḥ," the meaning is: because the Lord, who possesses power, is established precisely by a distinct means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
What is that? He says: "as stated. The word "hi" (for/indeed) should be joined after the word "sidhyann" (being established).
Regarding the term "inborn" (*sāṃsiddhika*):
since every object is included within the category of action, instrument, and result, it follows that the Lord must possess direct perception of all things as the basis for them all.
And because these [perceptions] are not produced by causes, the sense is that they are indeed eternal.
Regarding the phrase "of being an effect" (*kāryatvasya*):
the meaning is that there is a pervasion (*vyāpti*) such that wherever there is the state of being an effect, there is necessarily the production by a capable agent.
Even in the case of a potter and the like, there exist both ignorance regarding certain objects and incapacity.
The pervasion of "being an effect" (kāryatva) with respect to an agent who possesses little knowledge and little power is grasped through the force of observing repeated concomitance.

The author addresses the doubt that this [reason] is contradictory (viruddha) because it leads to a conclusion contrary to what is intended, by restating it with the words "But as for that... and so forth, and then refuting it with the word "that" (tat).
This is because it is non-conclusive (aprayojaka), meaning it lacks the capacity to bring about the production of the effect, due to factors such as ignorance regarding certain objects.

The meaning is as follows: the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) with respect to jars and the like is apprehended precisely by way of being preceded by an agent (*kartṛ*) as delimited by that specific form through which the potter's causality [toward the jar] is established.
Furthermore, the potter’s causality toward jars and the like does not consist in his possessing ignorance regarding some object;
rather, it consists solely in his being qualified by the capacity for direct perception and presiding over its material cause (*upādāna*) and so forth.
Knowledge or ignorance regarding other objects, or capacity or incapacity, are irrelevant to the production of the effect under consideration;
rather, the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*) is pervaded solely by the fact of being produced by a capable agent.
This is just as smoke has a necessary relation only with fire as delimited by its being qualified by conjunction with wet fuel.
But it is not [the case] with that which is delimited by irrelevant properties such as being red or being cow-dung; "like that" [refers to this].
He demonstrates the lack of probative force (aprayojakatva) itself with the words "for not," where "ignorance" means ignorance regarding the object, the means, and so forth.

"'Its own' means that only the capacity and so forth conducive to its own production is implied for the agent who is being inferred by virtue of being its own cause, because the property of being an effect is pervaded by having an intelligent agent."

The meaning is that a purely negative concomitance (*kevalavyatireka*)— that is, a negative concomitance consisting solely of the antecedent that is otherwise useless, namely the absence of capacity and so forth directed toward another object— is not established as the causal factor for the effect under discussion. Alternatively, the meaning is that the negative concomitance of the effect under discussion with the absence of capacity and so forth directed toward another object is unestablished, because the negative concomitance (*vyatirekasahacāra*) itself is unestablished.
The root text here might be otherwise;

[it means] "by that much alone," namely, by the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) itself which is conducive to its own production. It is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has an object (*viṣaya*) that is a different thing (*arthāntara*)."

The referent of the other word (*anyapadārtha*)—such as cognition and so forth—is established by implication; it is construed with the absence (*abhāva*) as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). [The term] "related" (*sambandhin*) refers to that which invariably precedes the effect.
"Of that which is ineffective" means of that which is not useful for the matter at hand—
that is to say, of that which is otherwise established.

Furthermore, by way of an alternative analysis, he rejects even the status of being an invariably antecedent factor for ignorance and so forth, which have other objects as their domain, with the words "Moreover" (*api ca*).

"Pervasive" means that which invariably precedes the effect. The point is this: the absence of the capacity for knowledge necessary for all effects other than the one under discussion is certainly not unestablished in the agent anywhere.
To the objection that it is both desired and observed that the agent lacks knowledge regarding certain objects other than the specific effect at hand, he says: "Now, however... (atheti).
Ignorance regarding some other object or something indeterminate is not established as a fixed state.

For example, just as one cloth-maker does not know a pot while another does, and one person does not know a certain thing while another knows it— so too, in the case of the agent under discussion, knowledge and ignorance regarding various different objects are seen to be unstable.

The meaning is that it is impossible to state with certainty that the ignorance of a cloth or the ignorance of a pot belongs to a specific agent; thus, because such ignorance is inconclusive (anaikāntya) with respect to various agents, it cannot serve as a logical reason (hetu).
Furthermore, he states "na cāsti" (nor does there exist... to show that it is indeed impossible to say that for every agent, some object is invariably unknown.
[Objection: But surely, ignorance is accepted as a reason by virtue of being the absence of knowledge qualified by itself (svaviśiṣṭajñānābhāvatva).
The term "svapada" (its own word) refers to the specific effect under discussion.

Furthermore, the state of being qualified (*vaiśiṣṭya*) in cognition [is defined] by the relation of both: not having its own inherent objectivity as a determiner (*anirūpaka*), and having an objectivity residing in something other than itself as a determiner.

Thus, even if there is deviation (*vyabhicāra*) for each respective instance of ignorance (*ajñāna*) in those respective cases, it is indeed possible for the absence of cognition delimited by the aforementioned form to invariably precede [the effect]. If this is argued:
Even so, it should be understood that the aforementioned "establishment through other means" (*anyathāsiddhatva*) remains unavoidable.

By this much, the objection that the nature of being an effect (*kāryatva*) implies a contrary form—such as being ignorant and so forth—with respect to the creator of the earth and other things, has been refuted.
Now, he refutes the objection that it implies a contrary form characterized by having a body, with the words "And not... (*na ca*).
It is not a fixed rule that the agent must possess a body;
for at that time, when the individual soul (jīva) abandons one body and takes up another body,
it is bodiless— this is the intended meaning.
The meaning is that when a yogi, by the power of yoga, takes on another body while still living, the soul (jīva) remains embodied at that time.
It is stated "of a non-yogi" because the taking on of another body by a yogi is observed to occur only while he is still possessed of his [current] body.
Now, one might object: even for a non-yogi, the assumption of another gross body occurs only for one who already possesses a subtle body (sūkṣma-śarīra).
Regarding the claim that there is no deviation [in the soul's departure] because of the word "having departed" (*pretya*), he says "the previous... [referring to the *pūrva* passage].
Now, one might object: by the force of scripture, the soul’s departure and so forth must be understood as occurring only when it is enveloped by the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*).
It is precisely these [elements], conjoined with the senses and the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), that are called the "subtle body" (*sūkṣmadeha*).
And if it is argued that there is thus no deviation (vyabhicāra) because the agent is necessarily possessed of a body, we reply:
even so, the lack of invariable concomitance (anaikāntya) remains established regarding the necessity of possessing a gross body (sthūla-śarīra).
However, for the subtle body, being a body in the primary sense does not apply;
yet, in a non-primary sense, this remains entirely unimpaired even for atoms with respect to the Lord.
For thus the Nyāya teacher Udayana maintains that atoms constitute the body of the Lord.

Having thus established that agency in the appropriation of a body belongs to the soul alone, even though it is bodiless, he says "Furthermore" (*kiñca*) to show that agency in the impelling of the body also belongs to the bodiless one alone. "Of the presiding one" (*adhitiṣṭhataḥ*) means of the one who sets [the body] in motion. "Entry into the body of the presider" (*adhiṣṭhātṛ-dehānupraveśaḥ*) refers to being a constituent factor of that which delimits the state of being a presider (*adhiṣṭhātṛtāvacchedaka*).
For one who presides over the body, the very volition (*saṅkalpa*) and so forth are what constitute the delimiter of the state of being a presider.
But that body [itself] is not [the locus].

The point is that just as wood or other material objects, which have become the object of an agent's presiding power (*adhiṣṭhāna*), do not possess the status of being the delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) for that presiding agent, so it is here.
[Objection: But how can the body, which is connected to its own presiding agent, not be the delimiting factor for that presiding agency?
Thus he raises the objection with the words "He presides over the two dark ones" (adhitiṣṭhāsite).
He refutes it with "Let there be one" (astveka).
The reading "ekatattve," found in earlier printed editions, is not correct.
The reading ‘ekatastvasaṃbaddhasya’ (of that which is not connected on one side) or some other variant may be possible;

however, since it is impossible for something absolutely unconnected with the object to be controlled to exercise control over it—just as it is impossible for an axe that is not connected to the wood to perform the act of cutting—there is this necessary rule: the controller must be connected with the object controlled.
The intended meaning is that [the soul] should not be considered as having a connection with the body.
He asks "Why? regarding the restrictive principle that the very relationship with the impeller (the Lord) is the cause for being impelled, and not the relationship with the body.
He answers this with "Since."
"Being presided over" means being set in motion;
[it is] by that which is connected to it, namely the impeller,
such as the hand, which is the qualificand here.
This is the intended meaning: there is no rule that only an embodied being can be an instigator, for even hands and other such parts can instigate measuring rods and the like.
Furthermore, it is possible that the status of being an instigator belongs only to that which is connected to the object to be impelled.

"Because even the hand and so forth [are causes] through their connection with that which is to be impelled. He raises an objection with "Now, if... The term "instigation" (*pravartana*) means the possession of an effort that prompts the activity of another.
And that [activity] belongs only to a person;
he, moreover, sets in motion the measuring rod and so forth by means of the operation of his own hand.

Thus, in the setting in motion of objects distinct from the body and its parts, there is necessarily a dependence on the operations of the body, hands, and so on. Therefore, the intention is that it is not possible for a formless God to be the director of atoms and the like.

He refutes this very rule by means of its lack of invariable concomitance (anaikāntya) with the words "that too is not so. The meaning is that since we observe the removal of poison from another's body and similar effects through mere mental operations— such as the meditation on Garuḍa as one's own resolve— even without the activity of the hands and other limbs, there is no fixed rule requiring dependence on bodily activity for a presiding agent distinct from the body and its parts.
It should also be understood that here, even the relationship between the impelled and the impeller occurs solely through the medium of cognition.
He raises a further objection with the word "how" (katham); the sense is that the body is the cause for produced cognition and so forth.
With an answer implied within it, he asks:
"What?"— meaning, what is the body's agency in volition (saṅkalpa), such that in its absence volition would not be possible?
He raises the doubt with the words "akaraṇam" (without an instrument).
To this, if it is argued that the body is the instrument there, we say no; the meaning is that the mind alone is the instrument.
And thus, the sense is that even in the absence of a body, volition (*saṅkalpa*) will arise from its own cause alone.

Now, if it is argued that although the mind is indeed an instrument (*karaṇa*), the body is still required as a limiting adjunct (*avacchedaka*) for produced knowledge (*janyajñāna*) and so forth, we reply: the requirement of the body exists only in the case of bound knowledge and the like, not elsewhere.

For, according to such passages as "He rejoices, beholding these desires with the mind alone in the world of Brahman" and "The creation of the world by the mind alone," both the liberated soul and the Lord possess a mind.
From that very [mind], cognition, volition, and so forth are perceived.
Even upon the departure of that body, since it is accepted that the mind possesses eternal sensory faculties, the occurrence of volition and other functions independent of a body is established.
Furthermore, in the view of the logicians who maintain that God possesses eternal knowledge, will, and effort, there is no dependence whatsoever on a body or the like.

In this context, it should be understood that the support for [the Lord] possessing a mind and having adventitious volitions and so forth is either according to the view of a partial school (ekadeśimatena) or under the guise of the final system (siddhāntacchāyayā).
With the words "But if this were so," he raises the objection of an undesirable consequence (aniṣṭaprasaṅga) regarding the possession of a mind;
the meaning is that since the state of possessing a mind is pervaded by [the states of] having a body and so forth, the Lord would consequently be subject to having a body and the like.
He refutes this, saying "Not so.

Since the pervasion of "being an effect" by "having a capable agent as its antecedent" has been grasped, it follows that from this [pervasion], when an agent is established for the earth and so forth, that agent—God—will be established precisely as being bodiless, omnipotent, and so on, according to the maxim: "The offering corresponds to the deity."
Furthermore, if one were to admit that [the Lord] possesses a body, it would follow that He lacks capacity;
how this is so will be explained immediately in the subsequent passage beginning with "And not for those such as us.

Thus, the consequence that the Lord would possess corporeality and a lack of sovereignty is contradicted by the very means of valid cognition that establishes His existence as the subject (dharmin). This is the meaning.
"By firmness alone" means by steadfastness alone.
The reading "by the very firmness of the meaning consisting in being produced by a capable agent" (*asamarthakartṛkatvārthadraḍhimnaiva*) is more excellent as a compound.
He also refutes the mind's being pervaded by corporeality and so forth with the word "of the mind."

The meaning is that even in the absence of a body—at such times as death or the intermediate dissolution (avāntaralaya)—the mind exists as a permanent sense-organ; therefore, the mind does not possess the property of pervading the body throughout time.

[Objection: Even so, since agency is observed in various places only for one who possesses a body, why is the pervasion of "being an effect" by "having a bodied agent" not apprehended? To this, he says: "For as long as... and so forth.

That which is observed to be consistent with the effect (*kāryānugama*) is therefore seen to be useful for establishing pervasion (*vyāpti*); thus, pervasion must be accepted as being delimited precisely by that form [of the cause] which is so observed.
Furthermore, it is only in the case of cognition (*jñāna*) and power (*śakti*) that there is consistency with the effect.
Even though these two depend upon the body in the case of a potter and others who are subject to karma;
The point is that by this much, the body and so forth do not enter into the category of the delimitors of pervasion (*vyāpakatāvacchedaka*).
In this way, the charge of including what is unintended has been avoided.
Now, he elaborates on the manner in which the intended specific [property] is established, beginning with the words: "And not for those like us."
Of that which is of infinite extent, of limitless depth, and of undivided scope, [he is] one whose body is localized, possessing a limited form existing within a restricted space.
*Alam* means capable.
The remainder is clear.
He raises an objection with the words "by such [a creator]":

the opponent's intention is that the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) of being an effect with a creator characterized by independence from karma, bodilessness, omniscience, and so forth, has not been observed in the case of a jar or similar objects.

With the underlying thought that the specific probandum belonging to the subject (*pakṣīyasādhyaviśeṣa*) is established through the apprehension of the pervasion delimited by a general property (*sāmānyadharmāvacchinnavyāpti*), aided by the force of the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatābala*), he offers a counter-objection with the words "in the extremely profound."
By means of the accuser's own words, he causes the opponent's defeat to be proclaimed with the phrase "of such a kind" (*yādṛśa*).
"Of such a kind" means having the form of a continuous, flowing stream that kisses the surface of the earth, which is exceedingly cold;
"of such a kind" refers to a great fire.
"‘Ta’diti” means "capable of producing smoke of such a kind as is capable of generating a great fire.
In this context, the reading might alternatively be the compound "tādṛśatatsaṃpādanasamartha" (capable of producing that which is such).
He states the analogy with the northern [example] in the words "this very [case].

Just as specific qualities such as place, time, and dimension are not included within the delimitor of the pervasion of smoke by fire because they are over-pervasive (*anaikāntya*), but rather only the nature of fire conjoined with wet fuel is so included; likewise, [in this case too].
In this way, even being human and so forth, though concomitant [with agency], is not included within the category of delimiters of agency;
for agency is observed elsewhere as well. Rather, it is mere capacity that is such [a delimiter]; thus he says, "Just as... and so on.
There is no difference between the inference of a specific fire on a mountain from smoke and the inference of a specific agent for the earth and so forth from their being effects;

the point is that just as the desired specific [agent] is established there, so it is in the present case as well. Now, wishing to raise a counter-argument by applying all properties merely because they are seen in a similar instance (sapakṣa), he says: "Moreover" (api ca).
By the phrase "conjoined with an all-pervading substance," the non-all-pervasiveness of the mind is intended,
because logicians do not accept the conjunction of two all-pervading substances.
The qualification beginning with "knowledge" is intended to establish the existence of the mind as the substratum of the conjunction that serves as the non-inherent cause of knowledge and so forth.
For in their view, it is the conjunction of the self and the mind alone that serves as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*) for cognition and other mental states;
and because cognitions do not arise simultaneously, that [mind] is held to be atomic (*aṇu*) and intangible (*niḥsparśa*).
Because if it possessed tangibility, it would follow that it is an element (*bhūta*);
and if it were an element, it would be impossible for it to perceive the specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of non-elements.
Here, the following counter-reasoning (*pratitarka*) is intended: if the mind were to possess a limited dimension or be possessed of motion, then it would necessarily be possessed of tangibility.
Furthermore, this is one example of how there may be deviation (vyabhicāra) even in that which has been observed to accompany [something] invariably.
Now, he demonstrates another example with the words "And how? (kathaṃ ca).
The word division is *aniyatādhiṣṭhānā*.

Although it is frequently observed that the great wind, being mobile and having an indefinite substratum, possesses manifested touch and is thus perceptible by touch, nevertheless, the skin-sense organ (*tvag-indriya*), which is inferred to be composed of air and pervades the body, is held to have a definite substratum and to be imperceptible by touch.
Herein lies the counter-argument (*pratitarka*): if the skin were a large effect produced from air, it would necessarily possess manifested touch and so forth.
Another illustration is given by the phrase "of the luminous" (*taijasasya*).
In the case of the luminous effect possessing the quality of magnitude (*mahiman*), there is the manifestation (*udbhūtatva*) of both color and touch, as in fire and the like;
whereas there is the manifestation of touch alone in cases such as the fire within a heated potsherd.

The meaning is as follows: although it is frequently observed that in light and so forth there is the manifestation of color alone, and likewise that both color and touch—or either one of them—are manifested, how is it that in the eye—which is inferred to be of a luminous (taijasa) nature because it manifests color alone among colors and other objects—there is no manifestation of those two? The undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) to be understood here is that if the eye were an effect of the mahat-tattva of fire (*taijasa*), there would necessarily be the manifestation of either color or touch.
With the intention of showing that these counter-arguments (*pratitarka*) are fallacious, the opponent replies with "Now" (*atha*).

[He does so] by referring to the frequent occurrence of those specific qualities—namely, the state of being perceptible through touch via either manifested color or touch, the state of possessing touch, and so forth.

The point is that, because the presence of [qualities] such as touch in the eyes and other sense organs is sublated by the non-perception of what is otherwise perceptible (*yogyānupalambha*) based merely on the observation of their co-existence, the probandum does not possess the pervasion of the probans.
Although it is difficult to state that the presence of touch in the mind is sublated by *yogyānupalambha* due to the mind's atomic nature,
nevertheless, if one were to accept its existence there, it would inevitably result in the violation of numerous established principles.
Thus he says: "the acceptance of that.
For example, if the mind possessed tangibility, it would follow that it is an element (*bhūta*).
If one does not accept its being an element, then the rule that "whatever possesses tangibility is necessarily an element" is violated.

Furthermore, if it is admitted that [the sense organ] apprehends what is real, then—just as with other senses—it follows that it cannot apprehend the specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of a non-real self.
Conversely, if it is admitted that it does apprehend them, then the rule that [a sense organ] cannot apprehend the specific qualities of what is unreal would also be violated.
Thus [it is argued].

In the same way, regarding the eye and other [senses], one should consider that if one were to accept their possession of manifested color (*udbhūtarūpa*) and so forth, there would follow the consequence of the collapse of various established rules.

Since there is no subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the contrary position (*vipakṣa*), the relationship of pervaded and pervader (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) between the thing to be established and the establishing reason is not proven.
Thus, it is intended to show that these counter-arguments (*pratitarka*) are "cut at the root" (*chinnamūla*).
The phrase "acceptance of such [a position]" means the acceptance of the intangibility (*niḥsparśatva*) of the mind (*manas*) and so forth.
The proponent of the doctrine of God (*īśvaravādī*), intending to show that by the same logic there is no fixed rule that being an agent entails having a body, says, "Well then, in that case...
This [statement] is intended to manifest joy born from having the opponent repeat back, through his own mouth, the very counter-reasoning (*pratitarka*) that was previously urged against him.
The word "hanta" [expresses a concession].
If God possessed a body, it would follow that He could be perceived through the medium of a body;
and if He were subject to succession, it would follow that He would lack omniscience and other such qualities.

Furthermore, omniscience and the like are impossible due to the absence of preeminent merit (*prakṛṣṭadharma*), because such merit cannot arise in the absence of the performance of the means for its attainment. Moreover,
on the position that this merit of the Lord is held to be eternal, the rule that merit in general is produced by enjoined actions would be violated.
Furthermore, if God were devoid of action, it would be impossible for Him to possess a body;
and if one were to accept that His body is eternal, the rule that having parts necessarily entails being an effect (kāryatva) would be violated.

Consequently, since even the earth and other such things would not be established as effects, the inference of God as their creator would be untenable—this is a point requiring extensive deliberation.

The intention [of the author] is this: the mere concomitance (*sahacāra*) of agency with having a body and so forth does not entail a necessary pervasion (*vyāpti*), because there is no subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the contrary case (*vipakṣa*).

Now, one might object: even though the eyes and other organs possess a luminous (*taijasa*) and other such natures, since their specific characteristics are established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it is impossible to apply a contradictory consequence to them.
If it is argued that the specific qualities belonging to God are not established by perception, he says "they are seen" (*dṛśyante*) in response.

"Reasonings" (*nītayaḥ*) means logical principles or inferences. The meaning is that there are indeed means of valid cognition regarding God's intended specific qualities. He elaborates on these very points with the words "just as" (*yathā*).
Regarding the reading "tathe" (thus): the syntactical connection is that "for thus are the principles seen.
"Thus" means those which establish the specific qualities desired by Īśvara.
Regarding Īśvara’s status as creator, that inference was stated previously. Of him—
Regarding its status as the creator, he says "the atoms and so forth.
The phrase "the subject of dispute" (*vivādāspadam*) is a qualification intended to indicate the possibility of being the subject of the thesis (*pakṣatā*);
for once there is a determination of either the probandum or its absence, the status of being the subject of the thesis ceases.
The meaning of that [phrase] "being the object of a disagreement regarding the possession of the probandum or its absence" results in:
"that which is being doubted as possessing the probandum."
The ancient masters maintain that the state of being a subject (*pakṣatā*) consists in doubt regarding the probandum (*sādhyasandeha*).

It should be understood that even in cases where [the probandum] is already established, inference occurs through the desire to infer (*anumitsā*), based on an induced doubt (*āhāryasaṃśaya*). Furthermore, instigation (*preraṇa*) is characterized by possessing a volition and effort conducive to the activity of another.

Having established that the Lord’s volition and effort have as their objects atoms and so forth, he establishes His direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) as being of the same nature by saying "in the same way" (*tathā*).
"In the same way" means just like the movement of a ball and such.
In the movement of a ball and such, the material cause (*upādāna*) is the ball and such.
The instrument consists of the stick and so forth.
One who directly perceives that [object] sets the ball and such into motion by means of the stick;
and from that, the activity toward it arises.

Thus, by means of the activity of atoms and so forth, as well as the activity of the self which is distinct from cognition and other such qualities, that which directly perceives the material causes, instruments, atoms, and the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) is here established.
And since this capacity for direct perception does not belong to individual souls (*jīvas*), there is no proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) by them.
Furthermore, the direct perception of even supersensible objects is the intended result of this inference.
Now, taking supersensible objects themselves as the subject (*pakṣa*), he establishes their being objects of perception with the words "perceptible.
That [subject] refers to atoms and so forth.
The intention of the supreme teachers who set forth such an inference is precisely this: that there exists someone who directly perceives supersensible objects.
He states the formal argument for the unity of the creator of earth and so forth in the words "by a single will. This collection of insentient phenomena is non-conscious.
Because it is non-conscious (acaityanya), that is, because it lacks sentience; it follows the will of a single conscious being, meaning it conforms to the volition of one sentient agent.
Here, one's own body serves as a positive example (anvayy-udāharaṇa). // 16 //

Those things which lack consciousness perform their function only when presided over by one [intelligent agent], because they act in dependence upon a connection with a body, like the skin and other such organs. (17)
The world, which is the subject of dispute, has a single primary person as its cause, because it consists of both sentient and insentient entities, like a kingdom ruled by a single king. (18)

Thus ends the *Īśvarasiddhi* (Proof of the Lord) within the *Siddhitraya*, graciously bestowed by the supreme teacher Śrī Bhagavad-Yāmunamuni, the preeminent upholder of the glorious Viśiṣṭādvaita doctrine.
Having established that the insentient manifold proceeds in accordance with the will of the Lord, he establishes the same for the sentient manifold as well with the words "by one.
[The phrase] "like the skin, etc. means like the sense organs such as the skin. // 17 //
He states the inference that establishes the specific qualities of being the lord of the entire world and the sovereign of all with the word "eka" (one).
That which has one primary person is "ekapradhānapuruṣa"; the meaning is "distinguished by one primary person."
The preeminence of the single Puruṣa consists in his being the controller and owner; the distinction [of the other] is characterized by being controlled and being subordinate. // 18 //
(Vyākhyā) Here, the refutation of the argument that "the Lord's agency is impossible because it would be purposeless," and so forth, should also be considered.
For instance: the Lord’s activity regarding the world is solely for the sake of protecting living beings.
[Objection: In that case, He should create a world consisting only of happiness.
It is not so;
for [the Lord] creates in such and such ways in dependence upon the karma of living beings.
[Objection: But if he depends on karma, would it not follow that his sovereignty is lacking? [Reply: No.

For just as a king who inflicts punishment in accordance with offenses is renowned for his supreme sovereignty, so too is God, who brings about the fruits of various actions, known for His preeminent majesty.
Indeed, His presiding over the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) and other factors constitutes His great glory;
and because He bestows fruits according to karma, His lordship over everything is firmly established in Him alone.

We infer that this is the intended meaning of the venerable teachers (Ācāryacaraṇa), who have presented proofs such as being the foremost of all and being the presiding deity of the unseen force (adṛṣṭa); this is the direction of our argument.
No further portion of the text is available to be found anywhere from this point onward;
therefore, I have composed this simple commentary on that which has been obtained.

Thus [ends the work] by the jewel among sons of the eminent preceptor named Śrī Kṛṣṇamācārya—a preeminent scholar who adorned the lineage of Prativādibhayaṅkarācārya and was born in the divine land of Śrī Nāgapurī (Tirunāṅgūra);

who has crossed to the further shore of the ocean of the four systems of philosophy; whose fame rests at the ends of the earth; who is an embodiment of compassion; who is a delighter in residing at Śrī Bhūtapurī, descended from the divine lineage of the venerable Bhāṣyakāra; and who is a sovereign among scholars.

May this *Siddhāñjana*, the commentary on the *Īśvarasiddhi* composed by the servant of the Śrīvaiṣṇavas, Prabhāvaṇṇaṅgācārya—who has mastered the heart of the systems of words, sentences, and means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) through service at the lotus feet of the preeminent teacher Rāmānujācārya, the venerable Hārīta Āsūri; who is a crest-jewel in Nyāya and Grammar; and who is a scholar in both Vedāntas—be ever victorious!
